    Industry News: ChatGPT Ads Hit 100,000 Advertisers – But Are They Seeing Results? via @sejournal, @brookeosmundson

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1596 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that openAI says more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT.
    • A recent Business Insider report found that some advertisers were struggling to earn back what they spent.
    • In September, advertisers were still trying to figure out what a reasonable click cost looked like on ChatGPT Ads.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that openAI says more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT. They’ve also reported that its ad business reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch.

    A recent Business Insider report found that some advertisers were struggling to earn back what they spent. Others reported results that matched or exceeded Google Ads.

    In September, advertisers were still trying to figure out what a reasonable click cost looked like on ChatGPT Ads. Now that some have had time to see what those clicks turned into, they’re deciding whether the results justify keeping the campaigns running.

    Business Insider cited Adthena’s findings from 30 enterprise brands that shared results between July and September. Adthena reported that 52% struggled to recover their spending, 26% matched or beat Google Ads, and 22% saw mixed results.

    Sources indicate that adthena gives little detail on how each brand measured returns or which Google campaigns it used for comparison. A brand comparing lead costs could come away with a very different answer from one comparing closed sales. With 30 brands sharing results, there’s only so much those percentages can tell you about what to expect in your own account.

    A LinkedIn poll I ran asked how people were using ChatGPT Ads. Of the 21 respondents, eight were still spending, and seven had tested and stopped. The other six wanted to test but couldn’t.

    Image from author, November 2026.

    In the comments, advertisers shared what they ran into once their campaigns were live.

    Melissa Mackey described the inquiries from her test as “junk leads.” Trevor Stolber tested the platform to prepare for client work and came away “very underwhelmed.” Leah Garcia stated creative drift was her main challenge at a moderate spend level.

    Brandi Benton ran into tracking issues during a short test and described targeting as “super limited.” Compared with Google Ads, she saw similar acquisition quality at a higher cost and with low volume. Her organic ChatGPT traffic brought in better-quality acquisitions than the ads. She intends to relaunch with upcoming creative and give the next test more time.

    I also had the opportunity to interview James Hamilton, co-founder of oakpool, a growth marketing agency and managed AI platform, about their ChatGPT Ads testing.

    In our discussion, he told me most clients who joined the agency’s ChatGPT Ads pilot are still spending. Oakpool has been running campaigns since spring for clients in boutique hospitality, B2B services, and entertainment. Hamilton said ROAS has been lower than on Google, but enough to keep a small budget running.

    According to recent reports, openAI’s conversion pixel has worked well for the hospitality campaigns, Hamilton stated, though he’d like more detail over time. He didn’t share spend or returns by industry. The results he described explain why clients have kept the campaigns running at their current budgets. How much more business those campaigns could bring in with additional spend is still open.

    Hamilton still gets more questions from clients about appearing in organic ChatGPT answers than about buying ads:.

    Our clients ask us far more often about earning a place in ChatGPT’s answers than about buying one. We expect that balance to shift as the ad product matures.

    Another agency advertiser said good organic results helped persuade some of its clients to try paid ads. Once the campaigns were live, some of those clients found that the ads brought in inquiries for work they couldn’t take.

    An agency advertiser who asked to remain anonymous spent about $15,000 on its own ChatGPT Ads in the first month. The campaigns worked well at first, then results dropped off. The agency now spends about $800 a month and treats that budget more like branding.

    Recent findings suggest that about half of the agency’s clients who tried ChatGPT Ads stopped and moved their budgets back to Google. The advertiser cited conversion tracking challenges and said it was hard to see where the ads appeared or why they showed up there.

    One client, a bankruptcy lawyer, saw up to 20 conversions a month at a low cost per lead. After two months, the campaign hadn’t brought in a single paying client. The inquiries were related to the firm’s work, but they fell outside the kinds of cases the lawyer wanted to take.

    According to recent reports, openAI’s pixel and Conversions API can help advertisers connect form submissions to their ads. For a firm in this position, the intake notes are where you’d look next. If several callers expected a service the firm doesn’t offer, was there something in the ad or landing page that gave them that impression?

    That’s something the team can check before spending more. If the offer was clear and the same inquiries kept coming in, it would help to know more about the conversations where the ads appeared.

    See also: Should Your PPC Strategy Focus On The Lead Pipeline Or Revenue?

    Gil Gildner noted approvals took weeks and sometimes months. His team broadened the campaigns to get them running. Clicks averaged less than $1 in the first week, but early delivery appeared to skew toward lower-income markets the client hadn’t planned to prioritize.

    In a recent development, the client had approved a sizable test budget, and Gildner doubted the team could spend it as planned. The first week gave him an average CPC for the traffic the campaign could buy. He still didn’t have a good sense of what clicks would cost in the markets the client wanted to test.

    In a recent development, A working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze examined 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking. In the U.S., visits from ChatGPT Ads generated $0.89 in revenue per session, compared with $2.45 for Google Search ads. The revenue figures alone leave out what advertisers paid for those visits.

    Say your Google Search campaign gets most of its conversions from people looking up your brand or checking prices. Using that CPA target for ChatGPT Ads assumes you’ll reach people who are just as ready to act. If you’re testing whether ChatGPT Ads can get your product onto a shortlist, a buyer might click weeks before they’re ready to book a demo. A CPA check at the end of the first week comes too early to account for those buyers.

    For a B2B team, this is where it helps to tag the ad links separately from organic ChatGPT referrals. If tracking connects the visits, the team can see that a prospect first came through an ad and later returned through Google to fill out a form.

    Keeping that earlier source in the CRM gives the team a way to follow the prospect past the demo request. It can check whether any of those leads became opportunities and how long that took.

    To find out whether the ads generated opportunities the business would have missed otherwise, the team would need to compare outcomes with and without the ads running.

    See also: Why Incrementality Testing Alone Won’t Fix Your Paid Media Budget – The Missing Metric.

    In a recent development, openAI’s technical breakdown explains how its ad system uses earlier messages to understand what someone is trying to do. The system uses that context to find relevant ads and weighs relevance alongside bids. As Search Engine Journal’s coverage of the auction explained, even an ad that wins the auction may never appear.

    Recent findings suggest that A B2B buyer might use ChatGPT to work out what features their team needs, then use Google to check vendor pricing. Matt Southern reported in September that people use both platforms. The audience overlap makes that path plausible. The research can’t tell advertisers whether an ad helped put a vendor on the shortlist.

    OpenAI notes advertisers don’t see users’ conversations. Even a broad breakdown of the types of conversations where ads ran would help, if OpenAI could provide it while keeping chats private.

    Industry observers note that A team seeing few demo requests could make a better call with that information. If people were still deciding what features they needed, the advertiser might try a landing page that helps them compare options. If the ads mostly appeared when people were already evaluating vendors, the team could check whether the page answered the questions buyers would have at that point, like what the product integrates with or how pricing works.

    If you ran ads on Facebook in the early days, you’ve seen how much an ad platform can change. ChatGPT Ads is still in its first year. Comparing a first test with an account you’ve spent years improving can make it easy to write off a campaign before you know what it can do.

    Industry observers note that some advertisers are already getting enough business from ChatGPT Ads to keep spending. There’s still little evidence that those results will hold across more advertisers or at higher budgets. And when a business knows why it keeps turning away the inquiries it paid for, giving the campaign another month is hard to justify without changing something.

    As ChatGPT Ads matures, better delivery reporting and conversion tracking could give advertisers a reason to revisit some of the tests they’ve paused. A team that couldn’t tell why its ads kept drawing the wrong inquiries might be able to go back with a more specific test.

    Until then, the results an advertiser can follow through to a sale or a qualified opportunity are a better basis for the next budget than the CPA from an account it’s been running for years.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    Our Sales team needs a dedicated data partner, and creator commerce (how creators monetize by selling digital products) is becoming a bigger part of how Kit and our creators scale. Kit is growing, so we're looking for a Senior Analytics Engineer to own Kit's sales and commerce data from end to end.

    Accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so important.

    It has been revealed that your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

    You'll build for two kinds of consumers: people and AI. Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    Industry observers note that sales and RevOps are your primary partners, who will rely on the models and reporting you own. You'll also partner with our Product team on reporting for features like Visual Automations and on how creators use Kit.

    Industry observers note that within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    First Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    According to recent reports, first Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Get familiar with how commerce data (products creators sell and the revenue they earn through Kit) lands in the warehouse today. Agree with RevOps and Sales on the most crucial questions they need answered. Review teammates' pull requests and contribute to our shared SQL, dbt, and documentation standards. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

    In a recent development, first Six Months: Ship and maintain well-tested, documented dbt models for core sales metrics, such as pipeline, deal velocity, stage conversion, win rates, and the sales-led funnel. Expose those metrics through the Omni semantic layer, working within the team's governance standards. Rebuild or refresh the core sales dashboards so pipeline reviews and forecasting conversations run on numbers that don't need manual reconciliation. Resolve competing sales metric definitions by writing down the options and tradeoffs, aligning with Sales and RevOps, and documenting the outcome. Model creator-level commerce data, such as products sold, revenue earned through Kit, and conversion, in partnership with data engineering. Write semantic layer descriptions, metric definitions, and documentation that let Omni's AI and MCP-connected AI tools answer routine sales questions correctly, and test them against real questions from Sales, RevOps and Product. Get Sales to the point where routine questions are answered through self-serve, whether in Omni dashboards, Omni's AI, or AI tools connected over MCP, rather than one-off requests.

    First Year: Be the recognized owner of Kit's sales data, the person Sales and RevOps go to first and trust without second-guessing. Give our revenue analysis work the sales and commerce models it depends on, so deeper questions about pipeline health and creator earnings can be answered promptly, thereby enabling us to make creators more successful. Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to latest teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer. Help raise the team's modeling quality through code review, pairing, and sharing what you learn.

    Deep dbt experience. You build modular, tested, documented dbt projects, and you're comfortable with incremental models, snapshots, macros, CI, and scheduled jobs in dbt Cloud or similar.

    Advanced SQL. You reason carefully about grain, joins, and window functions, and you write queries that are readable and performant on a cloud warehouse.

    In a recent development, data modeling for sales and GTM. You can model deals, pipeline stages and their history, ownership changes, and funnel conversion into clean, reusable structures. You are opinionated on Kimball standards and when a concept should be a fact or dimension.

    According to recent reports, CRM data fluency. You know how sales data behaves in a CRM, including stage changes, backdated edits, and custom properties. HubSpot is preferred, but other CRM experience (e.g. Salesforce) applies just as well. We care most that you recognize common CRM patterns.

    AI-assisted development. You use AI code editors and agents (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, or similar) every day, and you validate their output with tests, query results, and review before anything ships.

    In a recent development, clear written communication. You explain metric definitions, tradeoffs, and data caveats in plain language that Sales, RevOps, and Product partners understand.

    Industry observers note that BI and semantic layer experience. You can build dashboards and semantic models in Omni, Looker, or a similar BI tool, and you design metric definitions that people and AI tools can both query correctly.

    Recent findings suggest that git-based workflows. You keep pull requests small and well described, and you give thoughtful code review.

    Nice to have: Redshift performance tuning (sort and distribution keys), Python for scripting or API pulls, reverse ETL, and experience with product event, billing, payments, or ecommerce data.

    Around 7 or more years in analytics engineering or data engineering where you personally shipped production data models.

    Several years of hands-on work building and maintaining production dbt projects.

    Working directly with sales teams and RevOps, and owning reporting they relied on to run the business.

    Owning a data domain over time and evolving its models as the business and its questions changed.

    In a recent development, working at a SaaS tech giant, ideally one with both a self-serve and a sales-led motion. Commerce, payments, or creator economy experience is a plus, not a requirement.

    Working on a small or remote team where you were trusted to make decisions independently.

    It has been revealed that ownership and follow-through. You treat your data domains as yours. You notice problems before stakeholders do, close the loop on requests, and finish what you start.

    In a recent development, judgment. You match rigor to the decision at hand, know when a quick answer is enough and when a request should become a durable model, and say so clearly.

    Flexibility. You're glad to step outside your primary area when another team needs help, and you balance that work against your core commitments openly.

    According to recent reports, teach everything you know. You document as you go, pair generously, and help stakeholders understand the data well enough to use it on their own.

    Work in public. You share progress, open questions, and decisions in writing where the team can see them, including what didn't work.

    Creator success is our success. You remember who's on the other end. A wrong number in a pipeline review means Sales spends time on the wrong creators, and that shapes how carefully you work.

    In a recent development, do it with excellence. You test your work, review it carefully, and don't ship a number you can't defend.

    Candor with care. You're comfortable pushing back when a request won't answer the real question, and you do it in a way that builds trust.

    Needing detailed specs or a highly structured environment before you can start.

    Recent findings suggest that discomfort with ambiguity. Some of our sales and commerce definitions are still evolving, and you'll help settle them.

    Needing several layers of approval to make modeling decisions within your domain.

    Wanting to work only on dashboards, or only on pipelines, rather than across the transformation and BI layers.

    Recent findings suggest that wanting a strictly fixed scope. Sales comes first, but you'll pick up Product or other work when the business needs it.

    Wanting mostly greenfield work. Much of this role is improving sales models and dashboards that already exist.

    Preferring to take tickets as written rather than partnering with stakeholders on what they need.

    Being skeptical of AI's capabilities, or using AI without good judgment and accountability.

    Expecting a large data team with dedicated specialists for every part of the stack.

We work mostly on East Coast time - so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale.     We are hiring a Sr. Manager, Total Rewards to lead the design, delivery, and continuous improvement of Camunda’s global compensation, benefits, and equity programs. This person will partner closely with the People team, Finance, and Legal to make sure our rewards are competitive, equitable, compliant, and easy to understand in every country where we operate. This is a hands-on, strategic role for a rewards leader who wants to build and run programs as a trusted business partner, not just administer them. The right candidate will bring deep technical rewards expertise, strong AI and analytical skills, and a passion for a great employee experience. We also expect this leader to be AI-forward in how we approach compensation strategy and job leveling, not only in how they use AI to get their own work done. That means using AI and data-driven methods to shape pay philosophy, benchmark and model market data, design and calibrate our job architecture and leveling framework, and make faster, more consistent, and more transparent rewards decisions.

    Own job architecture, leveling, and grading frameworks, and keep the Job Catalog accurate as the company grows. Apply AI and data-driven approaches to job leveling, such as consistent role-to-level mapping, calibration, and level-drift detection, with human oversight.

    #135568. Industry News: AI Shopping Agents Bought A Fake Deal 37% Of The Time – Claude Opus Never Did via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (680 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: AI Shopping Agents Bought A Fake Deal 37% Of The Time – Claude Opus Never Did via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • AI shoppers trust the numbers a listing gives them.
    • Every present had a shelf of 10 listings, and one of them was the fake: a perfect 5.0 from tens of thousands of reviews, at a fifth to a quarter of everyone else’s price.
    • Each manufacturer had three models in the test, from its top model to a fast, cheap one.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    AI shoppers trust the numbers a listing gives them. Even when they wrote that a deal looked suspicious, they often bought it anyway, and never asked me about it. I sent nine AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, the companies behind Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, Christmas shopping 6,156 times. When one of the listings was an obviously fake deal, they bought it 37% of the time. Every purchase, with the reason the AI gave, is in the full study.

    Every present had a shelf of 10 listings, and one of them was the fake: a perfect 5.0 from tens of thousands of reviews, at a fifth to a quarter of everyone else’s price. For the scented candle, that was $6 and a 5.0 from 39,000 reviews, next to real candles at $24 to $40.

    Each manufacturer had three models in the test, from its top model to a fast, cheap one. The biggest surprise for me was the one that never fell for it:.

    I’m not sure why Opus never fell for it. My guess is something in how Anthropic trained it makes it look for this specifically, because the top models from OpenAI and Google both bought it. But I can only guess.

    Sources indicate that 315 times, an AI wrote that a deal looked suspicious, and 137 of those times it bought the fake anyway. That count is a floor, because some of the models don’t show their reasoning. Claude Sonnet wrote this just before buying a fake air fryer from Rushbeck, the made-up shop selling it:.

    “The price is so far below the rest that it could be a trap, but nothing in the data points to that, so I’m leaning toward Rushbeck.”.

    The AIs could ask me a question before buying. Across those 315 doubts, an AI asked me a question 10 times, every time about the size of the slippers, and never about the deal it doubted.

    It isn’t only shopping. Stanford researchers tested six chatbots on same-day news in February, and slipped a small false detail into some of the questions. Claude 4.5 Sonnet flagged the false detail 78% of the time, but still answered correctly only 46% of the time. GPT-5 answered correctly 19% of the time. Their paper also cites my AI user agents reference, in a note on how Grok’s crawler behaves.

    Recent findings suggest that the order of the 10 listings changed on every shopping trip, so each one was listed first equally often. When the fake was the one listed first, it was bought almost twice as often:.

    Every trip asked for a Christmas present within a budget, in one of three ways. Asked for the best value, the AIs bought the fake more than half the time, against 19% with no preference:.

    According to recent reports, I ran every shelf a second time without the fake. The 4.9-star listing won 2,277 of the 2,915 purchases, 78%. A real lower price won 16% and a full refund 4%. An award won 25 times and a crossed-out “was” price won once.

    So the rating decides, and the fake has a rating no real shop can match. This is mostly a warning for the shopper. A store can’t fix it, because it is very difficult to go from 4.9 to 5.0 while also massively increasing the number of reviews.

    One listing on every shelf carried a note hidden from people, telling AIs to choose it. It won 14 times across all 6,156 trips, all on one model, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite.

    I wanted to isolate just the choosing, as much as possible.

    I tested the models directly, not the ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude apps, which may add checks of their own. The full method is on the study page, and every request with every answer is on GitHub, free to reuse.

    If you let an AI do your Christmas shopping this year, check what it picked before you pay, and also what else was available.

    Industry News: Google Adds Pageburst & 11 Other Existing Bots To Its Crawler Docs via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that google identified pageburst as a user agent that renders pages to measure Google Ads quality and landing page safety and ignores robots.txt rules.
    • It has been revealed that pageburst is one of 12 existing user agents Google added to its crawler documentation on Nov.
    • “These crawlers and fetchers are not fresh; we’re documenting existing high-volume clients that are more likely to show up in server logs and that we’ve received questions about.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that google identified pageburst as a user agent that renders pages to measure Google Ads quality and landing page safety and ignores robots.txt rules. Its two strings look like a browser’s and do not contain “Googlebot”; a bot rule created using “Googlebot” will not capture them.

    It has been revealed that pageburst is one of 12 existing user agents Google added to its crawler documentation on Nov. 23, along with a corrected entry for APIs-Google. Google’s crawling documentation changelog explains:.

    “These crawlers and fetchers are not fresh; we’re documenting existing high-volume clients that are more likely to show up in server logs and that we’ve received questions about.”.

    The 12 belong to Google products other than Search, such as Google Ads, Gmail and Google Cloud.

    Google’s special-case crawlers page, which lists crawlers used by specific Google products, says pageburst “renders web pages for Google Ads quality, landing-page safety, and page understanding.” The entry adds that “it’s unaffected by crawling preferences.”.

    The desktop string identifies as Chrome on Linux and the mobile one as Chrome for iOS on an iPad, and both include “compatible; pageburst.”.

    Sources indicate that adsBot, which checks web page ad quality for Google Ads, has its own robots.txt token. Pageburst’s entry lists no token and says the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”.

    The highlights show what to look for in server logs and where Google states its robots.txt policy.

    It has been revealed that google’s documentation notes user-agent strings can be faked. Special-case crawlers use the IP addresses defined in Google’s special-crawlers.json; these have a reverse-DNS match of rate-limited-proxy-***-***-***-***.google.com. The pageburst entry does not say what occurs when a website blocks the Google Ads check.

    Besides pageburst, each of the five other newly documented special-case entries states the user agent “ignores robots.txt rules.”.

    Industry observers note that google’s user-triggered fetchers page covers the six newly documented fetchers and says that because a user requested the fetch, these fetchers “generally ignore robots.txt rules.” Three of those (AppEngine-Google, Google-Apps-Script and Google-Cloud-Tasks) send requests for code running within Google’s platform-based products. The remaining three are GoogleImageProxy, which is used to load image content into email applications such as Gmail, along with Google Web Preview and the PageSpeed Insights fetcher, both with strings ending in Chrome-Lighthouse.

    Several of the newly listed user agents seem to use standard browser strings. For example, a string from GoogleImageProxy appears similar to Firefox 11 on Windows NT 5.1; the strings for Google Web Preview and PageSpeed Insights, and one of PlayStore-Google’s, were created using Chrome strings. A filter that only identifies “Googlebot” would miss all of these.

    Sources indicate that google has moved APIs-Google, which makes requests to the webhook notification systems developers create within Google Cloud and Google Workspace APIs, from the list of special-case crawlers to the list of user-triggered fetchers. APIs-Google’s push requests, the changelog claims, “come from the user-triggered fetcher IP ranges and ignore robots.txt rules.” Google added a missing semicolon after “APIs-Google” in its documented string and tells developers to modify any code that was previously using a hardcoded version of the earlier string.

    Prior to the Nov. 23 enhancement, Google had included robots.txt as a method to block requests from APIs-Google in its documentation. In an Oct. 21 capture, the robots.txt token was present on the special-case page. On Oct. 30, a capture of the APIs-Google page showed “Use robots.txt” as one of two methods to block requests from APIs-Google. Now the APIs-Google page says that it “ignores robots.txt rules”; for controlling the delivery of notifications, the page points to either the developer who created the notification system or Google Cloud’s abuse form for unexpected requests.

    Recent findings suggest that pageburst renders pages for ads in Google and does not follow robots.txt. Check for “pageburst” in the log entries for your servers and CDNs, verify with Google’s procedures that the IP addresses are in its special-crawler ranges, and see if your pages were delivered to the verified requests, or if a challenge or a 403 was returned.

    Recent findings suggest that roger Montti covered Google’s advice on Nov. 18 that general bot blocking may keep Googlebot from crawling content when moving a CDN; the same advice should be applied to other Google clients that do not have the name Googlebot.

    Google’s special-case and user-triggered pages both say their lists aren’t exhaustive and cover the requestors “more likely to show up in log files.” The crawling documentation changelog, which is where Google logs additions like these, has an RSS feed.

    Tech Report: OpenAI Isn’t Planning Prompt-Level Reports For ChatGPT Ads via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • OpenAI doesn’t blueprint to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads.
    • Three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the company’s own AI agent.
    • OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting currently includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    OpenAI doesn’t blueprint to provide ChatGPT advertisers with reports showing the prompts or inferred intent behind their ads. When Adweek asked whether advertisers could expect such reports, Vijaye Raji, OpenAI’s CTO of applications, mentioned they should not expect them.

    Three executives who run OpenAI’s ad system told Adweek that ChatGPT ads are matched to search queries written by the company’s own AI agent. Advertisers don’t see those queries, only aggregate results.

    OpenAI’s basics page for advertisers explains that Ads Manager Beta reporting currently includes impressions, clicks, spend, CTR, average CPC, average CPM and conversions.

    OpenAI’s “About this ad” panel tells consumers why they saw an ad and what performance data advertisers receive.

    Recent findings suggest that openAI’s ad system begins by creating one or more search queries based upon buying intent determined from the conversation, per the tech giant’s ads engineering post published Oct. 21 by Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam. OpenAI calls the model that creates these search queries the orchestrator. Using these search queries, the ad system retrieves candidate ads, filters them, scores them and identifies the top candidates to be entered into an auction to set the price and select the winner. Returning no ad is called “an ordinary, successful outcome” in the post.

    As described in the post, if a user asks about a two-day Yosemite trip and then about a shoe brand’s latest product lines, the ad system may create a query representing that conversation such as “shoes appropriate for hiking trip,” even though the user did not connect the two questions.

    According to the post, when ads personalization is turned on, the orchestrator will also consider “nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations.”.

    ChatGPT owners in the European Economic Area and Switzerland will not have access to personalized ads at first, according to OpenAI’s ads FAQ for users. Brooke Osmundson covered the engineering post in October.

    Advertisers share context hints about where an ad might fit, and OpenAI indicates these hints help guide matching without determining it.

    OpenAI’s context hints guide claims:.

    Sources indicate that “Hints are not targeting rules or delivery instructions. They do not guarantee that your ad will appear for particular conversations, audiences, or situations, and they cannot enforce geographic limits, schedules, or exclusions.”.

    The basics page also says that hints “are not exact-match keywords.” Negative Phrases help qualifying advertisers limit where their ads appear, for “narrow placement requirements specific to their brand’s own policies.” The option is not necessarily available to every advertiser.

    Google explains that for some AI searches, the search terms provided in Google Ads reporting reflect the user’s intent rather than the exact query. According to Google’s ad group prioritization page, for searches done through Lens, AI Mode, AI Overviews and autocomplete, “the search term shown in your reporting represents the best approximation of the user’s intent.” Brooke posted about Google’s update to that page in May.

    OpenAI does not list a search terms report on its basics page.

    Recent findings suggest that chatGPT advertisers can determine what a campaign delivered, but they cannot see the conversations or queries that led to the results. Click-based and conversion-based campaigns can use the conversion tracking OpenAI supports through Ads Manager Beta. The basics page also describes how UTM parameters added to landing page URLs persist on ad clicks.

    OpenAI recommends writing your context hints in terms of customer needs and scenarios instead of listing keywords. Also, use OpenAI’s product controls where available to restrict delivery by geography.

    OpenAI says in its ads FAQ for users that it “may explore additional measurement insights over time while continuing to protect user privacy.” OpenAI sends new feature announcements by email to account holders. Check the reporting list on the basics page for updates.

    Coordinate developer-focused side events, meetups, and partner activations around major conferences.

    Collaborate with Partnerships on co-hosted events.

    Identify opportunities to scale successful initiatives across regions.

    Collaborate Across the Events Team.

    Partner with the events team on logistics and execution for community programs.

    Support promotion and event readiness with Marketing.

    Help ensure strong attendee experiences and post-event follow-up.

    Experience working with developer communities or technical audiences.

    Strong project management and organizational skills.

    Comfortable collaborating cross-functionally.

    Curious about developer ecosystems and the communities around modern infrastructure.

    Able to manage multiple initiatives in a fast-moving environmentComfortable working remotely and independently.

    Willing to travel for events as needed.

    Experience supporting developer meetups, hackathons, or workshops.

    Experience with community-led growth or developer advocacy programs.

    Experience running ecosystem or partner-led event programs.

    In a recent development, we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the organization. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Tech Report: What SEOs Can Be Thankful For: 8 Wins To Celebrate In 2026 via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate.
    • Search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility.
    • Recent findings suggest that this article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In SEO, we like to complain, but this industry and craft is also about finding the small wins to celebrate. Today is a day to consider what we are thankful for, so let us dig deep and create our SEO Thanksgiving list.

    Search may have given us plenty to navigate this year in AI, but Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI were each able to find their own ways to offer up some AI visibility. We can take the crumbs.

    Recent findings suggest that this article is the Search Engine Journal Thanksgiving list for all things SEO, social, local, and PPC. We finish off with a celebration for anybody who clicked their back button and went somewhere they had never been before.

    Google Search Console is presently displaying dedicated reports for your impressions in AI Overviews, AI Mode, and generative AI features in Discover, by page, country, and date. These newly introduced reports were released in June, and Google’s announcement now says, “As of August 31, 2026, we’ve rolled out these insights to all websites worldwide.”.

    We’re glad to finally see the AI impressions separated out from the normal impression totals.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide.

    Microsoft Bing Webmaster Tools added an AI performance report in February as a public preview, showing how many times Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summarizations, and some partner integrations reference your content, along with the referenced pages and the grounding query (the phrase used by the AI to retrieve the content).

    In June, Microsoft added a Citation Share feature in preview, which provides insight into what percentage of citations for a grounding query go to your site. The February report gives you a count of how many times you appeared in the citation list, and Citation Share reveals how large a piece of the pie those citations represent.

    SEJ covered it here: Bing Webmaster Tools Adds AI Citation Performance Data and here Google Search Console AI Reports Rolled Out Worldwide.

    According to recent reports, on Nov. 10, OpenAI introduced ChatGPT Business Hub in beta. All eligible businesses where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in Business Hub and, after claims and identity verification are approved, will be able to see mentions, website clicks, and discovery topics over the past 28 days.

    According to OpenAI’s setup guide for online businesses, a mention occurs when ChatGPT references your website, not if it just names your brand.

    In a recent development, vahan Petrosyan, director of technology for SEJ, submitted Search Engine Journal, and Business Hub showed 353,356 mentions and 2,663 website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10.

    Recent findings suggest that SEJ’s mentions and website clicks from Oct. 14 through Nov. 10. Screenshot by Vahan Petrosyan, Search Engine Journal.

    This is a beta version, and OpenAI indicates that claiming a business does not assure greater visibility within ChatGPT. However, these numbers are provided directly from ChatGPT, and mentions cannot be reflected in referral reports.

    SEJ covered it here: How to Submit Your Website to ChatGPT Business Hub.

    It has been revealed that google introduced platform properties for social and video accounts in July and made them available to everybody worldwide on July 29. They provide information regarding clicks, impressions, CTR and average position for posts on Instagram, TikTok, X and YouTube appearing in Google Search. Reports for Discover and Google News will also be displayed when applicable.

    The Insights report for a YouTube platform property shows clicks from Google Search over 28 days. Source: Google Search Central (CC BY 4.0, cropped).

    Your social team can now track how users locate the team’s social content on Google Search, within Search Console, the same tool utilized by your SEO team.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Search Console Adds Reports For Social Posts.

    Google announced the branded queries filter last November and made it available to all eligible sites by March. The branded queries filter allows you to sort your Performance report queries into branded, including misspellings, and non-branded, so you can identify traffic coming from customers searching specifically for your brand or products.

    In a recent development, the Search Analytics API got the same branded split this month. Prior to this branded queries filter being implemented, tracking traffic based upon specific branded searches required “maintaining complex keyword regex lists,” as Google put it. Many will agree that it is refreshing to no longer need such lists.

    SEJ covered it here: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    Google’s September Small Business Bulletin described view counts for Business Profile posts as “at the moment rolling out globally.”.

    Once the rollout has completed for your Business Profile, each post card located under the dashboard section will indicate views generated from Search and Maps activity for posts from the past 18 months.

    Google removed post metrics from Business Profiles in 2023. Now you can determine which posts receive the most views rather than making educated guesses. However, the bulletin said the counts were not accessible via the API yet.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Adds Post View Counts To Business Profiles.

    For PPC advertisers working in TikTok Ads Manager, the Q4 product preview highlighted Impression Share, a common metric seen in Google Ads, along with Top 1 Impression Share for Search Ads campaigns.

    Impression Share measures the percentage of eligible search results impressions that your ads capture. According to TikTok’s help section, availability of Impression Share may vary depending on account and market. Still, it can quickly reveal what portion of eligible search visibility you are leaving behind.

    TikTok also added Keyword Packs (pre-made brand and category keywords) to the Keyword Suggestion Tool for a faster way to create keyword lists.

    SEJ covered it here: TikTok Search Ads Adds Brand And Category Keyword Packs.

    Google began treating back button hijacking as a malicious practice in April and started enforcing this policy on June 15. Sites using back button hijacking could be subject to either a manual action or automated demotion.

    In a recent development, on Nov. 23, Google released a newly introduced FAQ which indicates the policy will apply if the back button hijacking occurs in a user’s browser, including when they visit your page via social media. Although this policy cannot eliminate all cases of back button hijacking, websites presently utilizing this tactic may want to stop.

    SEJ covered it here: Google Claims Back Button Hijacking Policy Covers Social Visits.

    Recent findings suggest that our single request for next year’s Thanksgiving holiday is the ability to differentiate Search Console’s AI clicks from web clicks. Currently, every time someone clicks on an AI Overview or AI Mode link, that click counts in the same Performance report as clicks on your other search engine results.

    Happy Thanksgiving from all the SEJ team.

    Featured Image: Zamrznuti tonovi/Shutterstock.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Curious about the kind of challenges you'll work on at Camunda? Watch this quick 30-minute talk from our engineers to learn more about the latest Camunda Exporter and how we’re solving complex problems at scale.

    In a recent development, we are looking for a Product Builder to join the IDP & RPA pod. You will take real problems from customers, decide what is worth solving, and build and ship the solution yourself, using AI tools to get from idea to production rapidly without lowering the bar.

    Product Building is how Camunda's Experience organization builds the applications people use on top of Camunda 8, such as Hub, Operate, and ProcessOS. Small pods of builders own a product area from customer problem to shipped change, with no hand-offs between product management, design, and engineering. We are setting this model up now, so you will help shape how it works.

    The IDP & RPA pod builds how Camunda processes work with documents and legacy applications. With intelligent document processing (IDP), customers create extraction and classification templates in Camunda Hub and publish them so a process can use AI to turn invoices and other documents into structured data. With robotic process automation (RPA), customers integrate legacy applications that have no APIs, using Robot Framework scripts on a standalone RPA worker. The hard problems come with putting LLMs into customer processes: extraction quality, model and prompt choices, testing and trust, and working for AI agents as well as for people.

    Help shape product direction for IDP & RPA by combining customer input, usage data, and field feedback into clear priorities.

    Partner with the other builders and product strategy to turn problems into shipped features, using short written proposals and prototypes to align early.

    Make judgment calls with incomplete information within your scope and own the outcome.

    Communicate trade-offs and decisions clearly to stakeholders who don't live in the details the way you do.

    Use AI tools across the whole loop, from specs to prototypes to production-ready code, and hold a high bar for what you ship by reviewing and improving the output rather than accepting it.

    Build, test, and ship improvements to the IDP & RPA experience, reading errors and tracing challenges far enough to give your pod useful context.

    Talk to customers and to support and customer success colleagues about how IDP is used and where it breaks, and turn what you learn into decisions about what to build next.

    Pick up customer incidents and trace them across Hub, the connectors, and the deployed process of the customer.

    Track what you ship against real outcomes and adjust when the data tells you to.

    Ability and/or willingness to use our product.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be.
    • Over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured swiftly.
    • What has not matured is the step before sampling.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The AI visibility industry has worked out how many prompts to track and how often to run them, and it still has no method for deciding which questions belong in the set or what a correct answer to any of them would be. That second problem is older than the first, and it has a documented solution that predates Google. Knowledge engineers have used it since the mid-1990s under the name competency questions, and it is almost absent from the conversation in search.

    Over the last year, the sampling side of prompt tracking has matured swiftly. Practitioners now broadly accept that a single run of a single prompt tells you very little, that branded and unbranded prompts have to be reported separately, and that wording changes results. The research supports the caution. A peer-reviewed study presented at ICLR 2024 found that formatting changes alone, with the meaning of the prompt untouched, moved one open-source model’s accuracy by as much as 76 points on standard benchmark tasks. That study tested benchmarks, not brands, but it establishes the underlying behavior: These systems respond to the form of a question as well as its content.

    What has not matured is the step before sampling. A scoping review posted this fall examined 38 empirical studies that query language models and measure outcomes for brands, and it judged that only five of them could defend how their prompts were chosen. Most used prompts written by the authors or generated by a model, with no evidence that those prompts represent what buyers ask. A separate survey makes the consequence plain: the prompts you pick, and the weight you give each one, define the market your visibility score describes, and that market may not match real demand. Both papers are preprints from single authors and have not been through peer review, so I treat them as a careful reading of the field and not as final findings.

    According to recent reports, the same review found that authors with a commercial stake in visibility services, or in a brand being measured, were behind 19 of those 38 studies. I am one of those people, since I founded CitationIQ, which measures AI visibility, and you should weigh what follows with that understanding (I was not part of any of those studies, for the record).

    The practical result is familiar to anyone who has sat in a prompt-selection meeting or had to choose them. Someone opens a spreadsheet, the team brainstorms questions, a tool suggests a few hundred more, and the list is frozen so that next month’s number can be compared with this month’s. Nobody writes down why each prompt is there, what business situation it stands for, or what the model would have to say for the answer to count as right. The score that comes out is precise, and its meaning is undefined.

    Industry observers note that in the early 1990s, Michael Grüninger and Mark Fox at the University of Toronto were building formal models of how enterprises operate, and they needed a way to decide what a model had to contain before anyone built it. Their answer, published in 1995, was to start with the situations the model had to support and then write the questions it must be able to answer in those situations. They called these competency questions because the questions define what the model is competent to do.

    It has been revealed that the thing they were building is called an ontology, which is easiest to relate to the knowledge graph you already know. The graph holds the facts, and the ontology is the blueprint those facts are organized by: what kinds of things exist, what properties they carry, and how they can relate. Schema.org plays that role for structured data on the web. Most entity work fills in the graph without stating what it must be able to answer, which is the gap competency questions close. From here on I will call the ontology a knowledge model.

    Recent findings suggest that A competency question is a question a knowledge model must be able to answer, written down before the model is built and used afterward to test whether it works. The questions come first, they come from real situations, and they double as the acceptance test. The Toronto method ran in six stages: Describe the motivating scenarios, write the questions informally, define the terms, restate the questions formally, write the rules, and then establish the conditions under which the model answers the questions completely. Later researchers borrowed test-first development from software engineering and turned the questions into tests that are written before the model is changed.

    Set that beside the spreadsheet. The knowledge engineer can trace every question to a scenario and every test to a question. The prompt list has no scenarios behind it and no expected answers in front of it.

    According to recent reports, it would be convenient to say that knowledge engineers solved this and marketers only need to copy them, and it would be wrong. A 2023 survey of 63 ontology engineers found that most of them use competency questions routinely, and that 77.8% have difficulty making sure their questions are both necessary and sufficient. Nearly two-thirds have trouble identifying questions that truly represent the scope, about half have trouble writing them properly, and two-thirds work with no guideline at all. Other researchers note that teams rarely publish their questions alongside the finished model, which means the requirements are often lost.

    I find that reassuring, not discouraging. Thirty years of practice has produced a clear record of where the method breaks: vague questions, questions nobody can check, question sets that drift away from the scenarios that justified them, and requirements that live in one person’s head. Those are the failures a prompt list has today, and the knowledge engineering literature has names and partial remedies for each of them. One recent classification separates scoping questions, which mark out what a model should cover, from validating questions, which check whether what it says is correct. That split maps directly onto the two things a brand wants to know: whether it appears in the answer at all, and whether what the answer says about it is true.

    The method does not transfer whole, and the reason matters. A knowledge model is deterministic: you run the formal query, and it returns the answer, or it does not. A language model is probabilistic, so the same question produces different answers across runs, phrasings, and engines, and the result is a rate instead of a pass or fail. You also do not own the thing being tested. A knowledge engineer who finds a failed question fixes the model, while you can only change the material the model draws on.

    According to recent reports, my adaptation, which is my own extension and not something the literature prescribes, is to run each competency question as two tests in a fixed order. First test your own content, which is deterministic: can a person find the expected answer, stated plainly, on a page you control or in a source you can influence? That is a pass or a fail, and you can fix a fail yourself. Only then test the language model by asking the question in several phrasings, several times, across the engines your buyers use, and recording how often the expected answer comes back. A critical survey of GEO research recommends three to five phrasings per information need, which is a sensible floor.

    The order matters because a language model that fails a question your own content cannot answer has told you nothing about the language model. In an earlier piece, I argued that AI visibility is three separate problems on three layers, and this is the diagnostic step that tells you which layer to look at. It also clarifies the relationship between a question and a prompt. The competency question is the requirement and the prompts are test cases for it, so twenty phrasings of one question are still one requirement, and a list of three hundred prompts may cover far fewer needs than it appears to.

    To make this concrete, take DuaneRoll, a payroll software tech giant I invented for this article. It sells to businesses with 50 to 500 employees, and its motivating scenario is a finance leader whose company has just hired in a third state and who asks an AI assistant what to do about payroll. Here are five competency questions for it.

    The fifth question is the one most prompt lists lack. An AI answer that credits you with a service you do not offer creates a support problem at best, and as I wrote about the German court rulings, an answer built from accurate facts attached to the wrong organization can become a legal one. Testing for what should not be stated is as much a requirement as testing for what should.

    Notice what the bad question has in common with most tracked prompts. It sounds like something a buyer would ask, it produces an answer every time, and the answer can be scored for sentiment. It fails as a requirement because there is nothing to check it against.

    Every expected answer above has a named owner, and that is deliberate. In knowledge engineering, a domain expert stands behind each expected answer. A prompt test usually has no such person, and the result gets pasted into a report with no record of which model, which version, which date, or whether web search was on. Sascha Donner, writing this year in the Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, argues that text from a language model lacks the testimonial grounding documents have always had, and that it becomes a usable document only when a person fixes it in a form and takes responsibility for it. The same applies to a test result. An expected answer needs a witness, meaning a named person who will say it is correct, and a logged result needs its conditions recorded, or it is an anecdote with a percentage attached.

    Recent findings suggest that once the questions exist, most of the measurement decisions make themselves. Each question states what to look for, each expected answer says what counts as correct, each owner says who to ask when the answer changes, and each scenario says why the question deserves a place in the set. Sampling, which the industry has learned to do well, then operates on a set that means something. A score built that way can be explained to a chief marketing officer in one sentence: Of the things buyers need to know about us, this is the share the engines get right.

    In a recent development, one caution before you hand the job to a machine. Asking an AI system to write your competency questions and grade the answers is tempting, and researchers are actively studying it. A study using 1,393 competency questions found that human evaluators’ performance dropped when the AI assistant gave them incorrect guidance. A language model can draft candidate questions quickly, and a person who knows the business still has to decide which ones are requirements.

    A competency question set for a brand is a short, owned list of what buyers must be able to learn about you, each item traceable to a real buying situation and paired with an answer someone will vouch for. Start with 10. Write the scenario, the question, the expected answer, and the owner; check your own content first, and only then look at what the engines say. The method is thirty years old, its weaknesses are well documented, and it is still more than most prompt lists have behind them.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes.
    • We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.
    • Industry observers note that we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale. Trusted by over 700 organizations worldwide, including 9 of top 10 US banks, Camunda helps enterprises boost operational efficiency, accelerate time-to-value, and deliver better customer experiences.Fully remote and global, we are in the middle of something bigger: transforming into an AI-first organisation, built on our own platform. We use Agentic AI to automate, orchestrate intelligent processes, and elevate human contribution across every team.Named GP Bullhound’s Top 100 Next Unicorn list, 2025 Great Place to Work certified. Visionary in 2025 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Business Orchestration and Automation Technologies. ranked 3rd in Flexa's 2026 Most Flexible Companies, We’re growing fast and looking for top talent to join our team. If you want meaningful work, visible impact and put something genuinely rare on your CV, keep reading.

    Hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

    Industry observers note that we are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

    You will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling newly introduced features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

    Camunda is an AI-first company, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

    This is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

    Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

    Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for latest features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

    Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce issues, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

    Recent findings suggest that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

    Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

    On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    What You Will Bring to the Role.

    Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

    Experience at a SaaS or software product firm, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

    Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

    In a recent development, threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

    It has been revealed that you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

    According to recent reports, you build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

    Clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

    Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

    Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

    Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

    Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

    Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

    Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

    This role is an existing vacancy.

    Recent findings suggest that we offer competitive, fair, and transparent compensation. Salary ranges are location-based, with Standard and Major markets (global tech hubs) reflecting local competition.

    The Annual Total Target Cash (base salary + 100% variable target, where applicable) shown below spans from the minimum in a Standard market to the maximum in a Major market. Final offers depend on skills, experience, and location, and we typically hire in the first half of the range to allow room for growth:.

    United States: $119,900.00 to $193,200.00.

    United Kingdom: £75,300.00 to £123,800.00.

    Singapore: S$148,900.00 to S$223,300.00.

    If you’re based elsewhere, you’ll be hired via Remote.com (our global employer partner), and your Talent Acquisition Partner will provide a personalized Total Rewards Calculator after your first interview.

    Equity: We also offer equity (where applicable) through our Virtual Stock Option Blueprint (VSOP).

    Industry observers note that we invest in your wellbeing, growth, and ability to connect, along with perks that support you no matter where you’re based. Our benefits are globally designed and locally delivered where applicable.

    Remote & Flexible: Work from anywhere with the setup that suits you, home office budget, co-working space support, and flexible time off to recharge when you need it.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    According to recent reports, health & Wellbeing: Access locally tailored healthcare, Modern Health for global mental wellbeing, and our Live Well Lifestyle Spending Account (LSA), a flexible, global benefit that puts you in control of your whole life, not just work, from: staying active, to caring for family, exploring personal passions, meaningful experiences, and investing in your financial wellbeing. The Live Well program debuts in 2026 and scales to €1,000 annually from 2027.

    Financial Security: Retirement and pension plans (often with firm contributions), plus life and disability insurance where relevant.

    Professional Growth: Up to $/€/£1,000 per year for self-driven learning: courses, certifications, books, you decide!

    AI in our hiring process: Camunda may use AI tools to aid the screening of applications and during the interview process. You can learn more here.

    Sources indicate that ”Everyone is welcome at Camunda” — it’s a celebrated component of our culture. We strive to create an inclusive environment that empowers our people. At Camunda, we honour diverse cultures and backgrounds and are proud to be an equal opportunity employer. All qualified applicants will receive consideration without regard to gender, race, ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, age, disability or any other protected characteristics under applicable law. We are looking forward to your application!

    Come join us and be part of Camunda’s incredible journey: Make an impact at a pivotal moment in our story!

    According to recent reports, please be aware that scammers may impersonate Camunda by reaching out about job opportunities. Camunda will only contact candidates from an email address ending in @camunda.com or @talent.camunda.com. We will never ask candidates for bank account details, checks, payment, or other sensitive financial information as part of our hiring process. If you receive a suspicious message, please do not respond, click any links, or share personal information.
